items.html:
Peruvian licence plates are either white or yellow. In contrast to the white plates, yellow plates are less likely to be seen.

Additionally, taxis in Peru typically use licence plates that are yellow on the top and white on the bottom.

NOTE: Within South America, yellow licence plates are only found in Peru, Colombia and rarely, Chile.

In Gen 3 coverage, Peru uses a solid black or white Google car.

NOTE: In South America, these two cars are limited to the following countries:

  • The black Google car is only found in Peru, Argentina and Uruguay.
  • The white Google car is only found in Peru, Bolivia and Chile.

An important thing to note is that Peru has Generation 4 Street View coverage, whereas the neighbouring country of Bolivia does not. While Ecuador does have some Generation 4 coverage, it will always have a large pickup truck.

Peru also has Generation 4 “smallcam” coverage, which is mounted lower than regular Generation 4 and has a relatively big circular blur with a small protrusion at the front.

NOTE: Peru, Brazil and Argentina are the only South American countries with smallcam.

Peruvian roads always have white outer lines. On highways, you will find either single yellow dashed or double yellow middle lines. On rural mountain roads, you will most likely see white outer lines without any centre line. On divided highways, the road lines may be completely white in colour.

NOTE: In the continent of South America, rural mountain roads, with the features mentioned above, are predominantly found in Peru.

Peru is the only South American country to use black-and-white striped signposts. In some areas, black-and-yellow signposts can be seen.

NOTE: Uruguay sometimes uses black-and-white posts for its traffic lights, but not for road signs.

Bollards in Peru are painted red or yellow, and the country mainly uses a variety of triangular-shaped concrete bollards. Occasionally you will also spot other designs, such as these circular concrete variants.

Black-and-yellow stripes on guardrails are seen throughout the country. You might sometimes find different designs, such as this sharp arrow design.

NOTE: Similar striped guardrails are also found in Bolivia. To differentiate them, just have a look at the outer stripe. Peru uses a black one, while Bolivia features a yellow one.

Kilometre markers in Peru are made out of concrete and are painted black and white.

NOTE: When entering and leaving urban areas, the markers will sometimes feature the road number.

Peruvian metal signposts feature concrete blocks at the bottom.

NOTE: Within South America, Peru is the only country to do so.

The country uses a variety of poles. They are made out of either concrete or wood, and sometimes feature distinct horizontal concrete bars.

NOTE: Horizontal concrete bars are also found in Argentina.

Some poles in Peru have painted bottom sections. Most commonly they will be black or black-and-yellow.

NOTE: This pattern of pole paint is unique to Peru within South America, however, similar ones can be seen in other South American countries, such as Colombia.
Bridges in Peru are commonly painted orange.
Peru largely consists of semi-arid mountain ranges and valleys.
Tuk tuks, called mototaxis in Peru, are frequently seen in the country, especially in major cities such as Lima, Trujillo, Chiclayo, Piura, and Iquitos.

Wide red and white stickers will typically be attached to the side of taxis and commercial vehicles.

NOTE: While less common, these can be found in some neighbouring countries.
Peruvian electricity counters have a unique design: They are rectangular, metallic, and typically feature two or three horizontal slits.

Sol is the currency of Peru. You will occasionally spot it on street view and its symbol is S/.

NOTE: The currency is unique to Peru.
Peru has many political party logos and all of them are unique to the country. Here is a list with other parties in Peru.

Peru is home to diverse and somewhat unique architecture. Here are a few examples of types of buildings commonly seen in Peru; ranging from Colonial-era buildings, contemporary “boxy” buildings, and traditional red brick buildings.

Some of these styles are broken down further in Step 2 of this guide.

Street View coverage in Peru is mostly located in the west and on main highways. There are some exceptions in the east near Iquitos and along the 30C.

_You can click on the image to enlarge it._

The country is generally flat in the east and mountainous in the west. However, an exception is the often flat desert near Piura in the northwest.

_You can click on the image to enlarge it._

Peru has a diverse climate, dominated by a dry desert in the west, and a tropical rainforest in the east.

_You can click on the image to enlarge it._

Highways in Peru are mainly located in the west, and the numbers increase from north to south. The 1, 3 and 5 are the longest and traverse through multiple departments.

_You can click on the image to enlarge it._

These three landscapes are typically found along offroads in Tumbes. You will always see sandy soil with either green or withered bushes.

NOTE: In addition, Tumbes does not have black cars on off roads. Make sure to consider it whenever you see such landscapes with a white Street View car.
The southwestern landscape of Piura is generally dry, featuring a low amount of vegetation with a few shrubs and bushes. The landscape is mostly flat, but you will sometimes see rolling hills.
Northwest of the city of Piura lies an area with similar vegetation to the area mentioned previously. However, this area is noticeably hillier.

Coconut palms (and other species of tall palms) can sometimes be seen in coastal areas of Peru, mainly north of Lima. They are mainly found in the agricultural areas which are typically found around the major coastal cities.
Olive tree plantations can be found in the far southern region of Tacna.

Most of the sugar cane production is found in the northern coastal regions of Peru near the cities of Chiclayo and Trujillo. Typically you see large fields of sugar cane in these areas. Smaller areas of sugar cane can be found further south in other valleys close to the Pacific coast.
Similarly to sugar cane plants, banana plants are generally found in agricultural regions adjacent to the coast in the northern half of the country.

A flat landscape in the mountains of Peru is usually seen in central Puno and around Lake Chinchaycocha.

NOTE: This landscape might look similar to Bolivia. Make sure to look out for other clues before guessing.
Low grass, a few hills, stone walls in villages and brown brick buildings are typical for the region south of Lake Titicaca in eastern Peru.
Far north Peru features mountains that are often covered in shrubby trees and bushes. Closer to the coast and the Ecuador border, these mountains are often quite dry in appearance.

Pine plantations are typically found in higher elevation areas of the country, away from the coastal deserts and Amazonian Regions. The most common types of pine trees planted are Pinus radiata and Pinus patula.
The areas adjacent to the northern Amazonian city of Tarapoto feature moderately tall foliage-covered mountains and can bear a similar resemblance to the hilly areas of Colombia or Brazil.

In higher elevation areas near the centre of the country, exposed rocky outcroppings are commonly seen in the sides of hills and mountains. Some areas with the highest concentrations are near Lago Chinchaycocha (Junin District) stretching south towards the city of Ayacucho.

NOTE: Exposed rocks can rarely be seen anywhere in the country, so use this meta with some caution.

Similarly, taller mountains near the middle of the country often feature rocky and sharp mountain tops. The main region of these mountains stretches from near the city of Huaraz southward to the city of Cusco; generally away from the coast.
Patches of light green lichen can be seen covering rocks and growing on the ground in high elevation areas of central and southern Peru.

Dark red-tinted soil is found in several areas of Peru. Some notable areas include the areas near Cusco and Ayacucho in the south of the country, as well as areas near the northern cities of Cajamarca and Tarapoto. It can be found to a lesser extent in adjacent regions.

Areas near the cities of Ica, Arequipa, and Tacna feature barren and mostly flat desert landscapes that can resemble areas of northern Chile. You can typically see mountains in the distance, primarily while looking to the east.

Coastal agricultural valleys in the middle and south are commonly sandwiched between dry mountains with no vegetation. The general orientation of these valleys are southwest-northeast.

NOTE: Agricultural valleys in the north of Peru can look similar, but often feature more shrubs and trees on the mountains.

As a general rule, the closer you are to Lake Titicaca in Peru, houses and buildings made out of red brick become more common. This type of architecture resembles the predominant type of building seen in parts of western Bolivia, which is helpful for remembering where it is seen most commonly. Additionally, buildings with blue tinted glass can be seen most commonly in the same areas.

NOTE: Red brick buildings can be seen anywhere in the country, so use other clues before guessing.
Buildings with overhanging roofs with wooden supports are mostly found in northern regions of Peru. These buildings are sometimes brightly coloured as well.

Pole markings with yellow vertical numbers are commonly found in northern coastal Peru and Tacna.

Oftentimes, but not always, they will be accompanied by a horizontal pole marking starting with a 2 or 3 letter code corresponding to a city. For example, this horizontal sticker starts with CH for Chimbote.

NOTE: you can further divide the region based on the number of digits and the actual numbers on the pole marking. See this document for details.

Tuk-Tuks with open front compartments are primarily found in the northern half of Peru, and are especially common in northern Amazonian adjacent regions.

NOTE: This type of Tuk-Tuk can be found elsewhere to a lesser extent, so use other clues before guessing.

Lamp posts in Lima and Lima Department often have a distinct, sweeping curve at the top, resembling an inverted "J" shape.

NOTE: This design can occasionally be found in other parts of the country, such as Iquitos and Pucallpa.

For other, more specific patterns, please see this document.
This cylindrical bollard, with a black and yellow stripe at the top, is unique to the state of Moquegua, which is located in the south of Peru.

The 1N near the Piura and Lambayeque border has a distinct looking landscape. It features a semidesert landscape and has overcast coverage in Generation 3. The new Generation 4 is drier but still looks somewhat similar.

Highway 1N/S is divided in the highlighted area on the map.

NOTE: It is the only divided highway outside of cities.

The 1S south of the city of Ica is not divided and mostly follows the coast. The soil is often red or orange in these areas, and there is little-to-no vegetation. This road is also entirely covered with the Generation 4 camera.
Ruta 5N between the towns of San Alejandro and Esperanza is a relatively straight, flat road in good condition. This road primarily runs north-south through the rainforest.

Ruta 30C in eastern Peru uses a white Street View car in Generation 3 between the cities of Planchon and Iñapari. It features dense forest, few villages, and resembles interior areas of Brazil. Some of this area has been overwritten with Generation 4. Most of this segment runs north to south.

Ruta 28B between the towns of Kimbiri and Echarate is a paved road with very faded or missing road lines. It is also characterised by being a relatively small road with Generation 4 coverage, which hugs the hillside and is located next to a river valley.

The valley connecting the cities of Jauja and Huancayo features a flat plain with plentiful trees, agricultural areas, and small villages. North-south oriented mountains can be seen on both edges of the valley.
The coverage on the north side of Lake Titicaca was taken during a significantly wetter season than the coverage taken on the south side of Lake Titicaca.

North of the city of Huancayo lies a shallow lake called Lake Chinchaycocha (also referred to as ‘the middle lake.’). This lake is generally marshy and a range of mountains can be seen to the east of the lake. This lake can look similar to Lake Titicaca, but is generally less densely populated and features fewer trees.

Volcanoes are often seen in and around the city of Arequipa.

NOTE: Within Peru, volcanoes are only found in the southeast in the highlighted area.
Most of the boulevard-type streets in Peru are in the city of Lima. These boulevards are typically long, straight streets divided by concrete or a grassy berm.

The east-central Amazonian city of Pucallpa, which lies close to the Brazil border, has a consistent street grid of WSW to ENE.

NOTE: Some northern and eastern areas of the city feature grids of different orientation.

Iquitos is a city in northeast Peru. It is an isolated city with only Generation 3 Street View coverage. Three-wheeled tuk-tuks, overcast skies, and rolling Amazonian landscapes are commonly seen in the area. This coverage is isolated from other areas of northern Peru.

The southern city of Cusco is recognizable by its prevalence of both red brick and Spanish colonial style buildings. Cusco is surrounded by mountains on all sides and features an airport in the middle of the city. Due to its proximity and similar architecture, Cusco superficially resembles the Bolivian city of La Paz.
The city of Tacna in the far south of Peru has this distinct dry ridge to the north.
Motorcycle taxi drivers in the Amazonian city of Puerto Maldonado can often be seen wearing yellow safety vests.
Within Peru, this white Street View car is found in central Cusco. It drives from the remote town of Aguas Calientes up to Machu Picchu.
A train track covered by a trekker is located between Aguas Calientes and Cusco.

lm.name: Landscape - Southwestern Piura Landscape
lm.note: The southwestern landscape of Piura is generally dry, featuring a low amount of vegetation with a few shrubs and bushes. The landscape is mostly flat, but you will sometimes see rolling hills.

lm.name: Landscape - Tacna Ridge
lm.note: The city of Tacna in the far south of Peru has this distinct dry ridge to the north.

lm.name: Landscape - Titicaca Villages

lm.name: Landscape - Volcanoes
lm.note:
Volcanoes are often seen in and around the city of Arequipa.

NOTE: Within Peru, volcanoes are only found in the southeast in the highlighted area.

lm.name: Trekker - Train Trekker
lm.note: A train track covered by a trekker is located between Aguas Calientes and Cusco.

lm.name: Vegetation - Palm Trees
lm.note: Coconut palms (and other species of tall palms) can sometimes be seen in coastal areas of Peru, mainly north of Lima. They are mainly found in the agricultural areas which are typically found around the major coastal cities.

lm.name: Vegetation - Pine Plantations
lm.note: Pine plantations are typically found in higher elevation areas of the country, away from the coastal deserts and Amazonian Regions. The most common types of pine trees planted are Pinus radiata and Pinus patula.

lm.name: Amazonas 8B
lm.note: Road 8B is a thin paved road (divided north of Chachapoyas) surrounded by distinct looking mountains. South towards the Cajamarca border the road runs along the edge of the mountain.

lm.name: Ancash 106
lm.note: Road 106 is a gen 4 dirt road in the Cordillera Blanca and is one of the most beautiful and easily recognizable roads in Peru.

lm.name: Ancash 1N Landscape
lm.note: Road 1N in Ancash (and parts of Lima) passes through a sandy desert landscape. A divided highway through desert with sand dunes is a good indicator of Ancash region.

lm.name: Ancash Foggy Roads
lm.note: Very foggy roads can be found in Ancash region, in the mountains west of Yungay.

lm.name: Ancash/LaLibertad Border Road
lm.note: The Ancash/La Libertad border road passes through dry, rocky mountains. Most of the road looks like this. While part of it is two lanes, the majority is a narrow, paved road.

lm.name: Apurimac 30A
lm.note: Road 30A cuts through a gorge. The entire road has overcast coverage, giving it a slightly dark appearance. The mountains are very recognizable.

lm.name: Apurimac 30B
lm.note: Road 30B is a thin, paved road with distinct-looking pavement, having darker lines a bit like Texas pavement.

lm.name: Apurimac Main Road 3S
lm.note: Road 3S in Apurimac, the main road between Ayacucho and Cusco, is a winding route along the edge of the mountains. Its elevated position overlooking a valley is a good indicator of Apurimac region.

lm.name: Ayacucho 28B
lm.note: Road 28B in Ayacucho region looks similar to the one in Cusco as it passes through tropical hills, but this section has road lines, unlike the more recognizable part in Cusco region.

lm.name: Ayacucho 30A
lm.note: Road 30A, between Nazca and Puquio, is a winding road passing through rugged, dry mountain ranges. Also these bollards are common along this road.

lm.name: Ayacucho 30A South
lm.note: East of Puquio lies a vast, open plain of arid terrain. It is sparsely vegetated with low-lying brown and beige scrub. Much of the coverage is very overcast and appears a bit dark.

lm.name: Ayacucho 30D
lm.note: Road 30D through central Ayacucho is a thin, paved, high-elevation mountain road. The landscape is very barren, similar to roads in Huancavelica region.

lm.name: Ayacucho 32
lm.note: Road 32 near Puquio is a thin mountain road. The northern section is a dirt road, while the southern section is paved. It has some bushes and shrubs, also rock walls are common along this road.

lm.name: Cajamarca 5N North
lm.note: The main roads in northern Cajamarca, near the Ecuador border, are mountainous, and pass through tropical vegetation.

lm.name: Cusco 113 Smallcam
lm.note: Cusco region has a few smallcam roads passing through the rainforest. Road 113, which leads to Manu National Park, is a narrow paved road surrounded by tropical vegetation.

lm.name: Cusco 28B
lm.note: The 28B is one of the most useful Amazonian roads to learn. The entire road runs along a river valley and has no road lines. Sections of the road are unpaved, but the majority is paved without road lines.

lm.name: Cusco 30C and Puno 34B
lm.note: These two roads descend through a valley of big tropical mountains. The roads are in good condition and have lots of bollards as well as yellow-black markings on guardrails. 34B drives north, 30C SW towards Cusco.

lm.name: Cusco Sacred Valley
lm.note: If you see steep, rugged brown mountains in a valley, you are probably in the Sacred Valley near Cusco, between Ollantaytambo and Pisac.

lm.name: Cusco South Gen 3
lm.note: This gen 3 coverage, with a white (or almost blurred-out) Google car, very overcast skies, and a wintery feel (often with snow on the mountaintops), is found in southern Cusco region between Sicuani and the Arequipa region border.

lm.name: Huanuco 14A
lm.note: Road 14A is a narrow, paved gen 4 road winding through hilly tropical vegetation.

lm.name: Ica Desert Roads
lm.note: Sandy gen 4 desert roads are most common in Ica region.

lm.name: Loreto Iquitos Road Pavement
lm.note: This dark asphalt pavement is almost on the entire road to Iquitos as well as in parts of the city, making it the easiest way to recognize the area. All roads in Iquitos are gen 3.

lm.name: Loreto Yurimaguas Road
lm.note: The road to Yurimaguas is mostly flat and tropical. It looks similar to the road to Pucallpa.

lm.name: MDD 30C
lm.note: Road 30C is a flat, well paved road passing through the rain forest. It has clear skies, unlike most other Amazonian main roads. On the southern section, the sky has an orange tint.

lm.name: Moquegua 108
lm.note: Road 108 is a gen 4 dirt road with sparse arid vegetation, including shrubs, bushes, and some cacti. Snowcapped mountains may also be visible.

lm.name: Moquegua 36A Road
lm.note: Road 36A in Moquegua has an arid landscape with scattered bushes and shrubs. Similar-looking terrain can also be found in Tacna and in south-western Ayacucho regions.

lm.name: Moquegua Ruta 1
lm.note: The coastal highway in Moquegua region runs north-south along the ocean and is quite winding.

lm.name: Pasco 18 Pavement
lm.note: This unique concrete pavement exists only on Road 18 in Pasco and Lima regions.

lm.name: Pasco 5N Dirt Road
lm.note: The section of the 5N passing through the mountains in Pasco region is a winding, unpaved dirt road (c2023). The only other roads that may look similar are the unpaved sections of the 28B, but the 5N is generally more winding and narrow.

lm.name: Pasco/Huanuco 5N
lm.note: Road 5N towards Pucallpa in Pasco and Huanuco regions is a mostly straight, north-south, flat road in good condition surrounded by tropical vegetation. Use road angle to find the right stretch.

lm.name: Piura 1N
lm.note: The eastern 1N road between Lambayeque and Piura regions runs straight NNW, with a significant mountain ridge to the east.

lm.name: Puno 38 Thin Road
lm.note: The southern part of Road 38 in Puno, which continues into Tacna region, is the only thin, paved gen 4 road in the region.

lm.name: Puno Divided Road
lm.note: The only divided road in the region connects Puno and Juliaca.

lm.name: San Martin 105
lm.note: Road 105, northeast of Tarapoto, is a thin paved road north of the mountains, running east-west through the rainforest.

lm.name: Tacna 40
lm.note: Road 40 climbs from Tacna to very high elevations, passing through a variety of landscapes. Parts of the route are unpaved, and you can see several volcanoes along the way.

lm.name: Tumbes Gen 3 Road
lm.note: The gen 3 roads through central Tumbes are easy to recognize. They are very dry, with sandy soil and a somewhat savanna-like landscape.

lm.name: Tumbes Main Road Landscape
lm.note: The main road in Tumbes runs parallel to the coast, with ocean to the north. To the south, you often see hills of light-colored, sedimentary soil, which are a good clue for Tumbes region.

lm.name: Ucayali 5N
lm.note: Road 5N from Tingo Maria towards Pucallpa is a very winding, somewhat hilly road with tropical vegetation. It looks similar to the road to Yurimaguas, north of Tarapoto.

lm.name: Ucayali Pucallpa Road 18C
lm.note: Road 18C is gen 4, flat, well-paved, and passes through tropical vegetation, sometimes including oil palms.

lm.name: Amazonas Mountains
lm.note: Mountains in this region are covered in green vegetation but have very visible rocky outcrops that give it a rugged appearance. These mountains are visible in most of the region.

lm.name: Ancash Cordillera Blanca Mountain Range
lm.note: Most of Peru’s snow-capped mountains are in the Cordillera Blanca mountain range in Ancash region, which also includes Peru’s highest peak, Nevado Huascarán.

lm.name: Ancash Gen 4 Landscape
lm.note: Ancash region has hilly landscapes with lots of eucalyptus trees.

lm.name: Ancash Mountains Roads
lm.note: Landscapes with big, rugged mountain peaks (some covered by snow) can be found in the Cordillera Blanca mountain range in Ancash.

lm.name: Apurimac Abancay Town
lm.note: The town of Abancay is surrounded by tall, brown mountains with sparse vegetation, visible from most parts of the city.

lm.name: Apurimac Gen 3 Landscape
lm.note: The gen 3 coverage near Andahuaylas is tricky. The landscape looks lush, similar to Cajamarca. The combination of very overcast skies, black gen 3 car, and tall eucalyptus trees is a good clue for this area.

lm.name: Cajamarca Gen 3
lm.note: Cajamarca region has dense gen 3 dirt road coverage. Lush looking landscapes with lots of eucalyptus trees. Many houses have metal sheet roofs that reflect the sunlight. Often fields are fenced off by tree rows, similar to Ecuador and southern Colombia.

lm.name: Cajamarca Gen 4
lm.note: Cajamarca is hilly with lots of eucalyptus trees and more lush than regions in the south. Buildings often have overhanging roofs with wooden supports.

lm.name: Cajamarca High Elevation Steppe
lm.note: Cajamarca region at high elevation can have this unusual for the region looking grassland steppe with sparse vegetation.

lm.name: Cajamarca Pines
lm.note: Pine tree plantations are most common in Cajamarca region.

lm.name: Cajamarca Town
lm.note: Cajamarca city can be identified by its abundance of northern-style roofs (overhanging with wooden supports) and white colonial-style architecture.

lm.name: Cusco Ausangate Mountain
lm.note: Recognizable mountain: Ausangate.

lm.name: Cusco City
lm.note: The town of Cusco has both red brick houses and white Spanish colonial-style buildings. It is surrounded by mountains. Buildings with orange or red tiled roofs are most common in Cusco region.

lm.name: Cusco East Landscape
lm.note: In southeastern Cusco, near the Puno border, there is a gradual transition between the rolling hills of the southern Altiplano and the slightly more forested landscapes of Cusco.

lm.name: Cusco South Landscape
lm.note: The far southern part of Cusco region has gen 4 roads across landscapes similar to Puno’s Altiplano. Some of the roads are wide without road lines, others are unpaved.

lm.name: Huancavelica Gen 4
lm.note: Most of Huancavelica region has high-elevation roads with rugged, barren mountains. Many of the roads are thin, paved mountain roads with white outside lines and no middle line. Almost entirely gen 4 2025.

lm.name: Huancavelica North/East Landscape
lm.note: Eastern and northern Huancavelica region has a different landscape, with river valleys that are at a lower elevation and have a bit more vegetation, like bushes and shrubs.

lm.name: Huanta Landscape
lm.note: Semi-urban landscapes with red soil dirt roads, some trees, prickly pear cacti, mud walls are common near the town of Huanta in northern Ayacucho region.

lm.name: Huanuco 2024 Coverage
lm.note: Huanuco region has gen 4 2024 rainy season coverage with lush hills and landscapes.

lm.name: Huanuco Town
lm.note: The city of Huanuco is surrounded by huge dark-green, barren mountains.

lm.name: Huanuco Unfinished Roads
lm.note: Unfinished roads (paved roads without road lines) are common in Huanuco region.

lm.name: Junin Huancayo
lm.note: Huancayo can be recognized by the huge mountains surrounding the city, as well as its grid.

lm.name: Junin Huancayo Valley
lm.note: The valley between Huancayo and Jauja is a flat plain with trees, agricultural areas, and villages. It runs at a NNW angle and is surrounded by mountains.

lm.name: Junin North Landscape
lm.note: Northern Junin, near Peru’s second-largest lake, has a more open landscape with rolling hills. This can look very similar to areas across the border in Pasco region.

lm.name: Junin/Pasco Landscape
lm.note: Junin and Pasco regions are located on the central high-altitude plateau, featuring grassy hills with almost no vegetation and exposed rock. Puno region can look similar, but it has less exposed rock.

lm.name: La Libertad Gen 3 Landscape
lm.note: Gen 3 hilly landscapes with lots of eucalyptus trees. Often dirt roads. The landscape can look similar to Cajamarca but it’s a bit less lush. Black gen 3 car is most common.

lm.name: Lima Gen 3 Landscape
lm.note: Gen 3 mountain dirt roads with dry, yellowish-brown grass and small shrubs/bushes are most common in Lima region. The sky is also often hazy. Gen 3 black car is most common.

lm.name: Pasco Cerro de Pasco
lm.note: Cerro de Pasco is a very high-elevation mining town. The buildings have metal sheet roofs, and the town is surrounded by rugged, barren mountains.

lm.name: Pasco Lakes
lm.note: Lakes on a very open, high-elevation, hilly, and barren landscape can be found in western Pasco region.

lm.name: Pasco Landscape
lm.note: Most of Pasco region lies on the central high-elevation plateau. The landscapes are similar to northern Junin: grassy plains with rolling hills and distant mountains.

lm.name: Pasco North Landscape
lm.note: Northern Pasco looks different from the rest of the region, featuring valleys through hills covered with eucalyptus trees.

lm.name: Pasco North Mountains Landscape
lm.note: Northern Pasco also has some higher-elevation gen 3 roads on hilly terrain with little to no vegetation.

lm.name: Piura East Landscape
lm.note: Eastern Piura looks similar to Cajamarca region: hilly terrain, many eucalyptus trees, lush vegetation, and houses with northern-style roofs. Many roads in Piura are unpaved. Political logos can also help differentiate the two regions.

lm.name: Puno 36A Bollard
lm.note: These bollards are unique to road 36A.

lm.name: Puno Gen 3 Landscape
lm.note: Puno has many gen 3 roads across a flat, high-altitude grass plateau with small hills and few trees. Red brick houses and stone walls are also common.

lm.name: Puno Gen 4 Landscape
lm.note: Puno region is located on a high-elevation mountain plateau (altiplano) and can be recognized by vast grassy plains and rolling hills with sparse vegetation.

lm.name: Puno Juliaca
lm.note: Juliaca is the largest town in the region and is flat, with a lot of red brick architecture. On gen 3 many of the roads inside the city are unpaved.

lm.name: Amazonas/Cajamarca Valley
lm.note: Near Bagua and Jaén, there’s a large open valley with surrounding hills featuring rice fields and palm trees. It may look a bit like the area near Tarapoto, but the mountains look different and the area is drier.

lm.name: Cajamarca Jaen Offroads
lm.note: Tropical mountain roads, often dirt roads, passing through lush vegetation are common near Jaén and up to the Ecuador border. The hills are bigger than in other Amazonian regions such as San Martin.

lm.name: Huanuco Tingo Maria Landscape
lm.note: Near Tingo Maria, the landscape is tropical, with large hills completely covered by trees. This differs from the area near Tarapoto, which has smaller hills with some green grass patches.

lm.name: Junin Amazonian Roads
lm.note: The Amazonian part of Junin region is hilly and tropical. It’s mostly gen 4, with 22 (if 22 amazonian then always Junin), 23 or 26 copyright.

lm.name: Loreto Iquitos Rural Roads
lm.note: Iquitos has a few rural roads west of town with very sandy soil.

lm.name: Loreto Iquitos Town
lm.note: Roads inside Iquitos have both the dark asphalt found on the road to Iquitos and concrete pavement. Transitions between these pavement types are often in poor condition.

lm.name: Loreto South Iquitos Pavement
lm.note: The far southern section of the road to Iquitos has a different pavement than the rest of the road. It can also be slightly hilly.

lm.name: MDD 30C Offroads
lm.note: Gen 3 rainforest dirt roads are side roads off the 30C. If it's flat you are likely near Puerto Maldonado, if it's hilly you are closer to the Brazilian border.

lm.name: MDD Bollards
lm.note: These sticks are only found on the 30C.

lm.name: Pasco Oxapampa
lm.note: Oxapampa features wooden elements reminiscent of architecture in the Alps (this type of architecture can only be found in Pasco and Junin). The town can also be recognized by the forested, tropical hills that surround it.

lm.name: San Martin Landscape
lm.note: San Martin region is hilly with lush tropical vegetation, it looks a bit like Colombia. The hills are often not entirely forested but have some grassy patches. If you have random tropical dirt roads with 2024 that are not flat, there’s a good chance you are in this region.

lm.name: San Martin Tarapoto Town
lm.note: Tarapoto is the largest city in the region. It is mostly gen 4 and somewhat hilly. If you are in a large tropical city with visible mountains, it’s likely Tarapoto.

lm.name: Ucayali Pucallpa Gen 3
lm.note: The majority of Pucallpa, especially the outskirts, is gen 3. These areas consist mostly of unpaved dirt roads with scattered houses and wooden fences. It looks very rural but is still part of the town.

lm.name: Ucayali Pucallpa Gen 4
lm.note: The center of Pucallpa is gen 4. It is flat and well-paved. Check Pucallpa’s grid to verify. A similar-looking city is Yurimaguas, north of Tarapoto.

lm.name: Ucayali Pucallpa Offroads
lm.note: Side roads off the road to Pucallpa are gen 4, flat, and mostly unpaved.

lm.name: Bollards
lm.note:
Bollards in Peru are painted red or yellow, and the country mainly uses a variety of triangularshaped concrete bollards. Occasionally you will also spot other designs, such as these circular concrete variants.

NOTE: These concrete variants can also be found in Bolivia and Brazil so do not rule out these countries if you find such bollards.

lm.name: Lima/Ica 1S Bollard
lm.note: These bollards are only found on the 1S highway between the towns of Ica and Lima.

lm.name: Moquegua Bollard
lm.note: This cylindrical bollard, with a black and yellow stripe at the top, is unique to the state of Moquegua, which is located in the south of Peru.

lm.name: North Lima Bollard
lm.note: This bollard is only found on the 1N highway north of Lima (still within Lima region).

lm.name: Tacna Bollard
lm.note: This bollard is almost exclusive to Tacna region. It does spill into Moquegua but it is by far most common in Tacna.

lm.name: Agricultural Valleys
lm.note:
Coastal agricultural valleys in the middle and south are commonly sandwiched between dry mountains with no vegetation. The general orientation of these valleys are southwest-northeast.

NOTE: Agricultural valleys in the north of Peru can look similar, but often feature more shrubs and trees on the mountains.

lm.name: Exposed Rock
lm.note:
In higher elevation areas near the centre of the country, exposed rocky outcroppings are commonly seen in the sides of hills and mountains. Some areas with the highest concentrations are near Lago Chinchaycocha (Junin District) stretching south towards the city of Ayacucho.

NOTE: Exposed rocks can rarely be seen anywhere in the country, so use this meta with some caution.

lm.name: Flat Desert
lm.note: Areas near the cities of Ica, Arequipa, and Tacna feature barren and mostly flat desert landscapes that can resemble areas of northern Chile. You can typically see mountains in the distance, primarily while looking to the east.

lm.name: Flat Valleys
lm.note:
A flat landscape in the mountains of Peru is usually seen in central Puno and around Lake Chinchaycocha.

NOTE: This landscape might look similar to Bolivia. Make sure to look out for other clues before guessing.

lm.name: Huancayo Valley
lm.note: The valley connecting the cities of Jauja and Huancayo features a flat plain with plentiful trees, agricultural areas, and small villages. North-south oriented mountains can be seen on both edges of the valley.

lm.name: Lake Chinchaycocha
lm.note: North of the city of Huancayo lies a shallow lake called Lake Chinchaycocha (also referred to as ‘the middle lake.’). This lake is generally marshy and a range of mountains can be seen to the east of the lake. This lake can look similar to Lake Titicaca, but is generally less densely populated and features fewer trees.

lm.name: North Piura Landscape
lm.note: Northwest of the city of Piura lies an area with similar vegetation to the area mentioned previously. However, this area is noticeably hillier.

lm.name: Northern Lake Titicaca
lm.note: The coverage on the north side of Lake Titicaca was taken during a significantly wetter season than the coverage taken on the south side of Lake Titicaca.

lm.name: Northern Mountains
lm.note: Far north Peru features mountains that are often covered in shrubby trees and bushes. Closer to the coast and the Ecuador border, these mountains are often quite dry in appearance.

lm.name: South Piura Landscape
lm.note: The southwestern landscape of Piura is generally dry, featuring a low amount of vegetation with a few shrubs and bushes. The landscape is mostly flat, but you will sometimes see rolling hills.

lm.name: Southern Lake Titicaca
lm.note: Low grass, a few hills, stone walls in villages and brown brick buildings are typical for the region south of Lake Titicaca in eastern Peru.

lm.name: Tall Rocky Mountains
lm.note: Similarly, taller mountains near the middle of the country often feature rocky and sharp mountain tops. The main region of these mountains stretches from near the city of Huaraz southward to the city of Cusco; generally away from the coast.

lm.name: Tarapoto Mountains
lm.note: The areas adjacent to the northern Amazonian city of Tarapoto feature moderately tall foliage-covered mountains and can bear a similar resemblance to the hilly areas of Colombia or Brazil.

lm.name: Tumbes
lm.note:
These three landscapes are typically found along offroads in Tumbes. You will always see sandy soil with either green or withered bushes.

NOTE: In addition, Tumbes does not have black cars on off roads. Make sure to consider it whenever you see such landscapes with a white Street View car.

lm.name: Volcanoes
lm.note:
Volcanoes are often seen in and around the city of Arequipa.

NOTE: Within Peru, volcanoes are only found in the southeast in the highlighted area.

lm.name: North - Overhanging Roofs
lm.note:
• Buildings with overhanging roofs with wooden supports are mostly found in northern regions of Peru.
  • These buildings are sometimes brightly coloured as well.

lm.name: South - Red Brick Transition
lm.note:
• As a general rule, the closer you are to Lake Titicaca in Peru, houses and buildings made out of red brick become more common.
  • This type of architecture resembles the predominant type of building seen in parts of western Bolivia, which is helpful for remembering where it is seen most commonly.

--- NOTE:

  • Red brick buildings can be seen anywhere in the country, so use other clues before guessing.

lm.name: Diverse Architecture
lm.note:
• Peru is home to diverse and somewhat unique architecture.

Here are a few examples of types of buildings commonly seen in Peru:

  • Ranging from Colonial-era buildings, contemporary “boxy” buildings, and traditional red brick buildings.

lm.note: Peru's electricity meters are rectangular and have horizontal rectangular openings. They look kinda like post boxes.

lm.name: Arequipa Town
lm.note: Arequipa has a distinctive colonial-style architecture, with arched windows and small overhanging roofs. Many houses in the old-town are built from sillar, a white volcanic rock. This cobblestone pavement is also quite common in the city.

lm.name: Lima Town
lm.note: A good clue for Lima is overcast weather, as other coastal areas often have clear blue skies. Boulevard-type streets are also mostly only found in Lima.

lm.name: Moquegua Ilo
lm.note: Moquegua’s second-largest city, Ilo, is a somewhat hilly coastal city surrounded by sand dunes.

lm.name: Moquegua Mountains
lm.note: The city of Moquegua is surrounded by rocky, light-colored, dry mountains. These mountains are also a good way to recognize Moquegua region.

lm.name: Piura Town
lm.note: The towns of Piura and Sullana can most easily be recognized by the abbundance of these mesquite trees, which are less common in coastal regions south of it.

lm.name: Tacna Sand Dunes
lm.note: Tacna is flanked by huge sand dunes on both sides of the city.

lm.name: Unique Guardrail
lm.note:
Black-and-yellow stripes on guardrails are seen throughout the country. You might sometimes find different designs, such as this sharp arrow design.

NOTE: Similar striped guardrails are also found in Bolivia. To differentiate them, just have a look at the outer stripe. Peru uses a black one, while Bolivia features a yellow one.

lm.map: A Learnable Meta Latin America - Beginner
lm.name: Black yellow stripes
lm.note: Black-and-yellow stripes on guardrails are common throughout Peru. Similar striped guardrails can also be found in Bolivia, but to differentiate them, check the outer stripe. Peru uses a black stripe, while Bolivia features a yellow one.

lm.map: A Learnable Meta Latin America - Beginner
lm.name: Concrete blocks
lm.note: Signs with concrete blocks at the bottom are unique to Peru in South America.

lm.map: A Learnable Meta Latin America - Beginner
lm.name: Sign post
lm.note: Black-and-white signposts like this are only found in Peru in South America. (If the signpost is inside a city, take this rule with a grain of salt, as you can rarely find them in other countries.)

lm.name: Arequipa vertical sticker
lm.note: A vertical white sticker with blue or red numbers places you in Arequipa Province

lm.name: Cloudless 30C
lm.note: The 18C and 5N road in central Peru, south and east from Pucalipa, and the 30C in eastern Peru, curving up to the Bolivian border, are pretty much the only places in the country with a flat profile (no visible mountains), a well-built road, and lush, jungly vegetation with a slightly yellow tint. You can tell which of the two you're on from the clouds: there aren't really any on the 30C, and the 18C/5N will always have substantial clouds.

lm.name: Cloudy 18C/5N
lm.note: The 18C and 5N road in central Peru, south and east from Pucalipa, and the 30C in eastern Peru, curving up to the Bolivian border, are pretty much the only places in the country with a flat profile (no visible mountains), a well-built road, and lush, jungly vegetation with a slightly yellow tint. You can tell which of the two you're on from the clouds: there aren't really any on the 30C, and the 18C/5N will always have substantial clouds.

lm.name: Cusco sideways pole numbers
lm.note: In the wider Cusco area and up to the tri-point with Brazil and Bolivia, concrete poles will sometimes have yellow stickers with black numbers going sideways.

lm.name: Hell road
lm.note: East of Chimbote, there's a road where sundown and clouds conspired to create footage as if from the depths (or rather heights?) of hell.

lm.name: Locumba bollards
lm.note: Around the town of Locumba, between Moquegua and Tacna, you get bollards that look like half-buried Moquegua type, interspersed with sections with just loose white rocks for bollards.

lm.name: Moquegua bollards
lm.note: These round white bollards with orange and black markings at the top are only found around the southern Department of Moquegua

lm.name: Moquegua-like bollards
lm.note: Bollards with the same color scheme as the Moquegua ones, but in different prism shapes (triangular, quadrangular) and/or with white and red reflectors appear on the 38A through Tacla and Puno and on the 3S south of Ilave. If they appear in Gen 3 coverage, go Ilo (on the coast)

lm.name: South sticker
lm.note: If you see a white sticker with blue text on a pole, you will be in the very south, below Arequipa

lm.name: Tumbes Vibes
lm.note: Sandy soil, fairly flat, green or withered bushes.

lm.name: Twin pole stickers
lm.note: Two horizontal yellow stickers with black text can be found on concrete poles in a corridor between Tingo Maria and Ayacucho.

lm.name: West Piura vibes
lm.note: Super flat desert (a bit hilly northwest though), sandy, sparse bushes

lm.name: Arequipa 1S Highway
lm.note: The 1S coastal highway in Arequipa region is a non-divided road that runs along the ocean and sometimes has a blur on one side of the image.

lm.name: Arequipa Camana/Punta de Bombon
lm.note: Agricultural fields surrounded by sand dunes on all sides except south can be found at the cities of Camana and Punta de Bombon.

lm.name: Arequipa Central Valley
lm.note: In central Arequipa region, at the cities of Majes and La Joya, there is a flat valley with small mountains in the distance. The valley has a lot of agriculture including prickly pear cacti fields.

lm.name: Arequipa Coastal Valleys
lm.note: Coastal valleys with dry, vegetation-free mountains are most common in Arequipa region. These mountains often appear smoother and lighter in color than those in northern coastal regions of Peru.

lm.name: Arequipa Colca Canyon
lm.note: The area near Chivay features the Colca Canyon along with snowcapped mountains and terrace-farmed agricultural fields.

lm.name: Arequipa Volcanoes
lm.note: Arequipa’s volcanoes, Misti and Chachani, are visible from much of the surrounding area.

lm.name: Arequipa Walls
lm.note: These brickly looking walls out of white volcanic rock are a good clue for Arequipa region.

lm.name: Ica Nazca Bollard
lm.note: Rectangular concrete bollards like these are only found around Nazca.

lm.name: Ica sand dunes
lm.note: Sand dunes can occasionally be seen in the city of Ica.

lm.name: Ica tar lines
lm.note: Roads covered with black tar lines are most common in Ica region.

lm.name: Ica trees
lm.note: Small, dead-looking trees by the road are another good clue for identifying Ica region.

lm.name: Ica tuktuks
lm.note: Ica uses tuktuks with closed compartments, unlike the cities in northern coastal Peru (Lima has both types).

lm.name: Ica/Lima 2025 valleys
lm.note: Valleys featuring rugged, dry mountains and 2025 copyright are mostly in Ica and Lima regions.

lm.name: La Libertad Landscape
lm.note: These light-brown, rugged mountains are more common in semi-coastal northern Peru, especially in La Libertad region. The valleys often have agricultural fields.

lm.name: La Libertad Sugar Cane
lm.note: Sugar cane fields stretch along the coast between Chiclayo and Lima, with the majority located between Chiclayo and Chimbote. Most are in La Libertad region.

lm.name: Lambayeque Coastal Landscape
lm.note: Flat landscapes with small canals and agriculture are most common near the city of Chiclayo.

lm.name: Lambayeque Hills
lm.note: Landscapes with some bushes, dry looking vegetation and scattered hills all around are mostly in Lambayeque region.

lm.name: Lima Hills
lm.note: On the outskirts of Lima, you can find these dry-looking mountains, often with many poor neighborhoods built on them.

lm.name: Lima/Ica Bollards
lm.note: These bollards are only found on the highway between Ica and Lima.

lm.name: Moquegua Bollard
lm.note: This bollard can only be found in the region of Moquegua.

lm.name: Moquegua North-East Landscape
lm.note: High-elevation, barren gen 4 desert roads with pale beige sand and almost no vegetation can be found in northeastern Moquegua, near the borders with Tacna and Puno.

lm.name: Peru Chincha Agriculture
lm.note: Northern Ica region is greener, with most agriculture concentrated around the town of Chincha. This area is mostly overcast.

lm.name: Peru Ica South Desert
lm.note: Southern Ica region has a desert landscape, a lot of it has dark looking soil.

lm.name: Peru KM Marker
lm.note: KM markers that start with PE are national roads. If they have 2 different letters they are regional and those letters are an abbreviation for the region name. They will also have a different color than black.

lm.name: Peru Region Poles
lm.note: Poles in Peru occasionally have the region name (or an abbreviation for it) written on them.

lm.name: Peru South Bollard
lm.note: This bollard is generally more common in the southern half of the country.

lm.name: Peru South Desert
lm.note: Non-coastal, flat, gen 4 desert landscapes are mostly found on the roads between Tacna, Moquegua and Arequipa. Use road angle to find the right stretch. Tacna has more red soil.

lm.name: Piura Coastal Gen 3 Landscapes
lm.note: Gen 3 landscapes with light grayish sandy soil and sparse vegetation are found near the coast in western Piura region.

lm.name: Piura East Dry Hills
lm.note: Eastern Piura region is hilly, with dry-looking trees and bushes. These arid hills are a good indicator for northern Peru.

lm.name: Piura NW Landscape
lm.note: Northwestern Piura has a similarly dry climate with sparse vegetation, but it is noticeably hillier, featuring rugged, eroded hills made of dry earth or sedimentary rock.

lm.name: Piura SW Landscape
lm.note: Most of Piura region has a very arid climate, with the only vegetation being scattered bushes and shrubs. Southwestern Piura is quite flat.

lm.name: Piura Trees
lm.note: Mesquite trees are very common in Piura region. They can also be found in Lambayeque, Tumbes, and Ica, but Piura has the highest abundance. Mesquite trees can also help identify Piura region in urban areas.

lm.name: Piura Valleys
lm.note: Near the town of Piura, there are a few valleys with some agriculture, though less than in regions south of Piura.

lm.name: Pole 1 Letter 4 Digits Horizontal
lm.note: Pole marking starting with an A followed by 4 digits are only found in Tumbes and Piura regions.

lm.name: Pole 6 Digits Vertical
lm.note: 6 digits vertical pole markings are common in Tumbes and Piura (can also be found in Lambayeque, Cajamarca and Tacna).

lm.name: Pole 7 Digits Vertical
lm.note: 7 digits vertical pole markings are common in Cajamarca, La Libertad and Ancash (rarely Piura, Lambayeque, Tacna). The code can start with 0 or another digit. If it's not 0 it tells you the region: 2 & 4 - Ancash; 3 - Cajamarca; 5 - La Libertad

lm.name: Pole 8 Digits Horizontal
lm.note: Only found in Piura region (very common in Sullana). Usually you won’t be able to see all the 8 digits (0000-0000). In Sullana sometimes you can find it with only 7 digits (000-0000)

lm.name: Pole 8 Digits Vertical
lm.note: 8 digits vertical pole markings are found in La Libertad region (rarely Cajamarca, Ancash)

lm.name: Pole 9 Digits Vertical
lm.note: 9 digits vertical pole markings are rare but can be found in Lambayeque (sometimes Ancash). Sometimes there are two letters instead of the first two digits.

lm.name: Pole Arequipa
lm.note: Red on white / blue on white digits vertical are common in Arequipa region. Rarely the red on white markings can be found in Lima.

lm.name: Pole Barcode Stickers
lm.note: These stickers are mainly in the regions of Tumbes, Piura, Ica and Lima. Differences: Lima - Big numbers in the middle; Ica - Readable numbers at the bottom; Piura & Tumbes: Very small numbers at the bottom.

lm.name: Pole Black Warning Sign
lm.note: This is the most common style of the warning stickers in the northern half of the country.

lm.name: Pole Callao
lm.note: In Callao you often find a light blue - dark blue painted section at the bottom of the poles.

lm.name: Pole COMOL
lm.note: Most of the COMOL poles are found in Arequipa region (rarely in Cusco).

lm.name: Pole Double Horizontal
lm.note: Very long horizontal Pole markings. Common in Junin, Pasco and Huanuco (sometimes Ayacucho, Huancavelica). Typically, the shorter code starts with a 4. The next two letters refer to the region you are in.

lm.name: Pole ENOSA
lm.note: Definitely most common in Piura but Tumbes also has them.

lm.name: Pole ENSA
lm.note: Can be either in the form of a sticker: blue text on white background with black border or in a form of regular marking similar to company name markings. Useful for getting Lambayeque.

lm.name: Pole Horizontal Letters
lm.note: 3 Letters and 3 Digits horizontal pole markings. The letters are an abbreviation for nearby towns (scannable!). Can also be 2 letters, 4 digits. Useful to memorize: CJ - Cajamarca; HI - Trujillo; EN - Chiclayo; CH - Chimbote

lm.name: Pole ICASAC and HHSAC
lm.note: ICASAC are in Ica (rarely Ayacucho) region. HHSAC are in Ica (rarely Huancavelica) region.

lm.name: Pole LDS
lm.note: LDS poles are unique to Lima region.

lm.name: Pole Pucallpa Sticker
lm.note: In the city of Pucallpa you can often find poles with this combination of these four stickers.

lm.name: Pole Rotated Vertical
lm.note: These rotated numbers markings are only found in Apurimac, Cusco and Madre de Dios. In Cusco, you can sometimes find it with other rotated markings.

lm.name: Pole Support
lm.note: Poles with support can be found in the south, most common in Puno, Cusco and Apurimac. Poles without support can be found in the north, most common in Cajamarca.

lm.name: Pole Tacna/Moquegua
lm.note: These blue on white divided markings are only in Tacna and Moquegua regions. Colors can sometimes be inverted as white on blue.

lm.name: Pole White kV Stickers
lm.note: White kV stickers can be found in Lambayeque, Cajamarca (rarely Amazonas) regions. The letters on these stickers may refer to the nearby city’s name. For example: JAE - Jaén.

lm.name: Pole Yellow kV Warning Sign
lm.note: These yellow warning stickers which contain information about voltage (kV) are unique to Ica region and very common.

lm.name: Political Logos Amazonas
lm.note: If you see one of these logos you are in the region of Amazonas.

lm.name: Tacna Bollard
lm.note: This bollard with these reflectors at the top is only found in Tacna region (except for a small spill into Moquegua region on the main highway).

lm.name: Tacna Gen 4 Desert Dirt Roads
lm.note: Tacna region does have some gen 4 desert dirt roads, but they are more common in Ica region.

lm.name: Tacna Olive Trees
lm.note: Olive tree plantations in Peru are found almost exclusively in Tacna region. If you see them you are likely south west of Tacna.

lm.name: Tumbes Gen 4
lm.note: Gen 4 roads in Tumbes often have dense, somewhat dry vegetation, including cacti and some palm trees. The landscape can look a bit like northeastern Brazil.

lm.name: 1 Letter and 4 Digits (horizontal)
lm.note: 1 letter and 4 digits (horizontal) (X0000 / X-0000) This marking is only found in Tumbes and Piura and should always start with an A. (it is often accompanied by other regional markings like "6 Digits Vertical") Credit to peru pole doc (desc)

lm.name: 1S South of Ica
lm.note: The 1S south of the city of Ica is not divided and mostly follows the coast. The soil is often red or orange in these areas, and there is little-to-no vegetation. This road is also entirely covered with the Generation 4 camera.

lm.name: 2025 Copyright
lm.note: This will get updated and I will remove it/update the meta if it does. But currently (march 2025), 2025 copyright is only found here. (theres like one road in the north that has it also but looks nothing like this area) Ty to ritchie

lm.name: 5m Poles
lm.note: Poles with 5m written on the bottom of them are only found in the north of the country. Especially in Tumbes, Piura and La Libertad. Credit to Peru poles doc (desc)

lm.name: 6 Digits Vertical
lm.note: This one is common in the far north provinces of Tumbes and Piura, but can also be found in Lambayeque, Cajamarca and Tacna. It is usually paired with other regional markings. Credit to peru pole doc (desc)

lm.name: 7 Digits (vertical)
lm.note: This type of pole marking is most common in Cajamarca, La Libertad and Ancash. It can also be rarely spotted in Piura, Lambayeque and Tacna. Markings in the northern provinces can either have a solid black border, dashed black border or no border while in Tacna it will always be no border. Sometimes, instead of the first two digits there will be two letters (XX00000). If it starts with 2 or 4, it is Ancash. If it starts with 3, it is Cajamarca. 5, is La Liberdad. (Cred. to Pole doc (desc)

lm.name: 8 Digits (vertical)
lm.note: When you see this one, it should be in La Libertad, although I was able to find one in Cajamarca and in Ancash. cred. to peru pole doc (desc)

lm.name: Arequipa Vertical Sticker
lm.note:
A vertical white sticker with blue or red numbers places you in Arequipa Province.

Credit to wayfinder

lm.name: Arequipa Volcanoes
lm.note:
Volcanoes are often seen in and around the city of Arequipa.

NOTE: Within Peru, volcanoes are only found in the southeast in the highlighted area.

lm.name: Banana Plants
lm.note: Similarly to sugar cane plants, banana plants are generally found in agricultural regions adjacent to the coast in the northern half of the country.

lm.name: Coastal Agricultural Valleys
lm.note:
Coastal agricultural valleys in the middle and south are commonly sandwiched between dry mountains with no vegetation. The general orientation of these valleys are southwest-northeast.

NOTE: Agricultural valleys in the north of Peru can look similar, but often feature more shrubs and trees on the mountains.

lm.name: Coconut Palms
lm.note: Coconut palms (and other species of tall palms) can sometimes be seen in coastal areas of Peru, mainly north of Lima. They are mainly found in the agricultural areas which are typically found around the major coastal cities.

lm.name: Cusco
lm.note: The southern city of Cusco is recognizable by its prevalence of both red brick and Spanish colonial style buildings. Cusco is surrounded by mountains on all sides and features an airport in the middle of the city. Due to its proximity and similar architecture, Cusco superficially resembles the Bolivian city of La Paz.

lm.name: Cusco sideways pole numbers
lm.note:
In the wider Cusco area and up to the tri-point with Brazil and Bolivia, concrete poles will sometimes have yellow stickers with black numbers going sideways.

Credit to wayfinder

lm.name: Divided 1N/1S
lm.note:
Highway 1N/S is divided in the highlighted area on the map.

NOTE: It is the only divided highway outside of cities.

lm.name: Ensa/9 Digits (vertical)
lm.note: 9:This one is less useful as it’s quite rare but can be spotted in Lambayeque and rarely in Ancash. Similarly to the 7 digit version, sometimes there will be two letters instead of the first two digits (XX0000000). Ensa: Can be either in the form of a sticker: blue text on white background with black border or in a form of regular marking similar to company name markings. Useful for getting Lambayeque. Both are common on the same pole, which will place e you in Lambayeque. credit to pole doc (desc)

lm.name: Far North Peru
lm.note: Far north Peru features mountains that are often covered in shrubby trees and bushes. Closer to the coast and the Ecuador border, these mountains are often quite dry in appearance.

lm.name: Flat Desert Landscape
lm.note: Areas near the cities of Ica, Arequipa, and Tacna feature barren and mostly flat desert landscapes that can resemble areas of northern Chile. You can typically see mountains in the distance, primarily while looking to the east.

lm.name: Flat with Distant Mountains
lm.note:
A flat landscape in the mountains of Peru is usually seen in central Puno and around Lake Chinchaycocha.

NOTE: This landscape might look similar to Bolivia. Make sure to look out for other clues before guessing.

lm.name: Hell Road
lm.note:
East of Chimbote, there's a road where sundown and clouds conspired to create footage as if from the depths (or rather heights?) of hell.

Credit to wayfinder

lm.name: Ica Barcode
lm.note: Ica stickers look very similar to Tumbes/Piura stickers but the numbers below the barcode are significantly bigger and most of the time you should be able to read at least some of them. Rarely, Ica stickers can be spotted in Ucayali or Loreto. Cred to peru pole doc (desc)

lm.name: Ica Yellow KV Stickers
lm.note: In the province of Ica, the stickers contain information about voltage (kV) just under the warning text. Here you can see some examples: Note that it only applies to this specific design with no additional text apart from the warning and voltage information. cred to peru pole doc (desc)

lm.name: ICASAC
lm.note: As the name would suggest, most common in Ica, although also findable in Ayacucho. cred to peru pole doc (desc)

lm.name: Iquitos Vibe
lm.note: Iquitos is a city in northeast Peru. It is an isolated city with only Generation 3 Street View coverage. Three-wheeled tuk-tuks, overcast skies, and rolling Amazonian landscapes are commonly seen in the area. This coverage is isolated from other areas of northern Peru.

lm.name: Juaja to Huancayo Valley
lm.note: The valley connecting the cities of Jauja and Huancayo features a flat plain with plentiful trees, agricultural areas, and small villages. North-south oriented mountains can be seen on both edges of the valley.

lm.name: LDS
lm.note: LDS poles are unique to the Lima Province and Lima Region but they are way more common in Lima Province. Credit to Peru Pole doc (desc)

lm.name: Lichen
lm.note: Patches of light green lichen can be seen covering rocks and growing on the ground in high elevation areas of central and southern Peru.

lm.name: Lima Barcode
lm.note: This type of stickers can be spotted in both Lima Region and Lima Province. Unlike Tumbes/Piura and Ica stickers, Lima stickers have the numbers in the centre of the sticker and the barcode below them. Sometimes there is no barcode at all. The numbers are also even bigger than on the Ica stickers. cred to peru pole doc (desc)

lm.name: Lima Boulevards
lm.note: Most of the boulevard-type streets in Peru are in the city of Lima. These boulevards are typically long, straight streets divided by concrete or a grassy berm.

lm.name: Machu Picchu Car
lm.note: Within Peru, this white Street View car is found in central Cusco. It drives from the remote town of Aguas Calientes up to Machu Picchu.

lm.name: Machu Picchu Trekker
lm.note: A trekker around Machu Pichu walks up a lot of stone stairs. There is lots of foliage, but you can often make out the iconic mountains and ruins.

lm.name: Middle Lake
lm.note: North of the city of Huancayo lies a shallow lake called Lake Chinchaycocha (also referred to as ‘the middle lake.’). This lake is generally marshy and a range of mountains can be seen to the east of the lake. This lake can look similar to Lake Titicaca, but is generally less densely populated and features fewer trees. I also mistitled the tag but I don't have the will to fix it right now.

lm.name: Moquegua Bollard
lm.note: This cylindrical bollard, with a black and yellow stripe at the top, is unique to the state of Moquegua, which is located in the south of Peru. (It also only seems to appear on the 36A)

lm.name: North Lake Titicaca
lm.note: The coverage on the north side of Lake Titicaca was taken during a significantly wetter season than the coverage taken on the south side of Lake Titicaca.

lm.name: Northern Roofs
lm.note: Buildings with overhanging roofs with wooden supports are mostly found in northern regions of Peru. These buildings are sometimes brightly coloured as well.

lm.name: Northern Tuk-Tuks
lm.note:
Tuk-Tuks with open front compartments are primarily found in the northern half of Peru, and are especially common in northern Amazonian adjacent regions.

NOTE: This type of Tuk-Tuk can be found elsewhere to a lesser extent, so use other clues before guessing.

lm.name: Olive Tree Plantations
lm.note: Olive tree plantations can be found in the far southern region of Tacna.

lm.name: Pine Plantations
lm.note: Pine plantations are typically found in higher elevation areas of the country, away from the coastal deserts and Amazonian Regions. The most common types of pine trees planted are Pinus radiata and Pinus patula.

lm.name: Piura
lm.note: The southwestern landscape of Piura is generally dry, featuring a low amount of vegetation with a few shrubs and bushes. The landscape is mostly flat, but you will sometimes see rolling hills.

lm.name: Pucallpa
lm.note:
The east-central Amazonian city of Pucallpa, which lies close to the Brazil border, has a consistent street grid of WSW to ENE. All of the coverage in the city was taken with the Generation 3 camera.

NOTE: Some northern and eastern areas of the city feature grids of different orientation.

lm.name: Red Brick
lm.note:
s a general rule, the closer you are to Lake Titicaca in Peru, houses and buildings made out of red brick become more common. This type of architecture resembles the predominant type of building seen in parts of western Bolivia, which is helpful for remembering where it is seen most commonly. Additionally, buildings with blue tinted glass can be seen most commonly in the same areas.

NOTE: Red brick buildings can be seen anywhere in the country, so use other clues before guessing.

lm.name: Red Soil
lm.note: Dark red-tinted soil is found in several areas of Peru. Some notable areas include the areas near Cusco and Ayacucho in the south of the country, as well as areas near the northern cities of Cajamarca and Tarapoto. It can be found to a lesser extent in adjacent regions.

lm.name: Rocky Outcroppings
lm.note:
In higher elevation areas near the centre of the country, exposed rocky outcroppings are commonly seen in the sides of hills and mountains. Some areas with the highest concentrations are near Lago Chinchaycocha (Junin District) stretching south towards the city of Ayacucho.

NOTE: Exposed rocks can rarely be seen anywhere in the country, so use this meta with some caution.

lm.name: Ruta 28B
lm.note: Ruta 28B between the towns of Kimbiri and Echarate is a paved road with very faded or missing road lines. It is also characterised by being a relatively small road with Generation 4 coverage, which hugs the hillside and is located next to a river valley.

lm.name: Ruta 30C
lm.note: Ruta 30C in eastern Peru uses a white Street View car in Generation 3 between the cities of Planchon and Iñapari. It features dense forest, few villages, and resembles interior areas of Brazil. Some of this area has been overwritten with Generation 4. Most of this segment runs north to south. (Im pretty sure its basically all gen 4 now so idk how usefull the car meta is, but the road is still distinct)

lm.name: Ruta 5N San Alejandro to Esperanza
lm.note: Ruta 5N between the towns of San Alejandro and Esperanza is a relatively straight, flat road in good condition. This road primarily runs north-south through the rainforest.

lm.name: Sharp Mountain Tops
lm.note: Similarly, taller mountains near the middle of the country often feature rocky and sharp mountain tops. The main region of these mountains stretches from near the city of Huaraz southward to the city of Cusco; generally away from the coast.

lm.name: South Sticker
lm.note:
If you see a white sticker with blue text on a pole, you will be in the very south, below Arequipa

Creedit to wayfinder

lm.name: South Titicaca
lm.note: Low grass, a few hills, stone walls in villages and brown brick buildings are typical for the region south of Lake Titicaca in eastern Peru.

lm.name: Sugar Cane
lm.note: Most of the sugar cane production is found in the northern coastal regions of Peru near the cities of Chiclayo and Trujillo. Typically you see large fields of sugar cane in these areas. Smaller areas of sugar cane can be found further south in other valleys close to the Pacific coast.

lm.name: Tacna Ridge
lm.note: The city of Tacna in the far south of Peru has this distinct dry ridge to the north.

lm.name: Tarapoto Area
lm.note: The areas adjacent to the northern Amazonian city of Tarapoto feature moderately tall foliage-covered mountains and can bear a similar resemblance to the hilly areas of Colombia or Brazil.

lm.name: Train track
lm.note: A train track covered by a trekker is located between Aguas Calientes and Cusco.

lm.name: Tumbes Offroads
lm.note:
These three landscapes are typically found along offroads in Tumbes. You will always see sandy soil with either green or withered bushes.

NOTE: In addition, Tumbes does not have black cars on off roads. Make sure to consider it whenever you see such landscapes with a white Street View car.

lm.name: Tumbes/Piura barcode
lm.note: In these two provinces the main part of the sticker is the barcode. Under the barcode you can notice some numbers, but most often they will be too small to actually read them. This particular design can rarely appear in other provinces so use with care. Credit to Peru Pole doc (desc)

lm.name: White Kv Sticker
lm.note: The letters on these stickers refer to the nearby city’s name. For example: JAE - Jaén. I have also found Kv stickers in Tumbes(extremely rare). Credit to Peru pole doc (desc)

lm.name: With Support: Four Rectangles Poletop
lm.note: It only applies to this specific poletop with three horizontal bars and one vertical that resembles four rectangles. With a support bar is found in the South. The support together with the first horizontal bar can form a triangle or a trapezoid. cred to peru pole doc (desc)

lm.name: Without Support: Four Rectangle Pole Top
lm.note: It only applies to this specific poletop with three horizontal bars and one vertical that resembles four rectangles. This Poletop without the support is only in the north. Cred to peru pole doc (desc)

lm.name: Roadlines
lm.note:
• Peruvian roads always have white outer lines.
  • On highways, you will find either single yellow dashed or double yellow middle lines.
  • On rural mountain roads, you will most likely see white outer lines without any centre line.

--- NOTE:

  • In the continent of South America, rural mountain roads, with the features mentioned above, are predominantly found in Peru.

top.html:
Peruvian licence plates are either white or yellow. In contrast to the white plates, yellow plates are less likely to be seen.

Additionally, taxis in Peru typically use licence plates that are yellow on the top and white on the bottom.

NOTE: Within South America, yellow licence plates are only found in Peru, Colombia and rarely, Chile.

NOTE: In South America, these two cars are limited to the following countries:

  • The black Google car is only found in Peru, Argentina and Uruguay.
  • The white Google car is only found in Peru, Bolivia and Chile.

top.html:
Peru is the only South American country to use black-and-white striped signposts. In some areas, black-and-yellow signposts can be seen.

NOTE: Uruguay sometimes uses black-and-white posts for its traffic lights, but not for road signs.

top.html: Bollards in Peru are painted red or yellow, and the country mainly uses a variety of triangular-shaped concrete bollards. Occasionally you will also spot other designs, such as these circular concrete variants.

Occasionally you will also spot other designs, such as these [circular](https://www.google.com/maps/@-14.4839611,-70.9887188,3a,24.9y,19.81h,72.8t/data=!3m6!1e1!3m4!1sU37DGxXpc0hXg0BPOLhRRw!2e0!7i13312!8i6656) concrete variants.

top.html:
Black-and-yellow stripes on guardrails are seen throughout the country. You might sometimes find different designs, such as this sharp arrow design.

NOTE: Similar striped guardrails are also found in Bolivia. To differentiate them, just have a look at the outer stripe. Peru uses a black one, while Bolivia features a yellow one.

top.html:
Kilometre markers in Peru are made out of concrete and are painted black and white.

NOTE: When entering and leaving urban areas, the markers will sometimes feature the road number.

Peruvian metal signposts feature concrete blocks at the bottom.

NOTE: Within South America, Peru is the only country to do so.

top.html:
The country uses a variety of poles. They are made out of either concrete or wood, and sometimes feature distinct horizontal concrete bars.

NOTE: Horizontal concrete bars are also found in Argentina.
top.raw: The country uses a variety of poles. They are made out of either **concrete** **or** **wood**, and sometimes feature distinct horizontal concrete bars. NOTE: Horizontal concrete bars are also found in Argentina.

top.html:
Some poles in Peru have painted bottom sections. Most commonly they will be black or black-and-yellow.

NOTE: This pattern of pole paint is unique to Peru within South America, however, similar ones can be seen in other South American countries, such as Colombia.
